How to read the notation

Character tokens are separated by one space. Each / token represents exactly one original ASCII space. Original LF line breaks remain line breaks. A {lc} prefix marks a lowercase letter, preserving its original case. Unsupported characters, including non-ASCII punctuation, appear as {U+XXXX} Unicode code-point tokens. These prefixes and escape tokens are edition notation, not alphabet signals. Every source text character is accounted for, and decoding this notation restores the exact extracted text.

International Morse uses dots and hyphens for letters A–Z, accented É, digits, and the listed punctuation. The source slash / becomes -..-.; a bare / token is a space. Lowercase a–z and é use a {lc} prefix followed by their uppercase signals. No accent stripping, smart punctuation replacement, or other transliteration occurs. × is escaped to distinguish it from X. This is a written encoding, not timed audio or a radio transmission.
